audience: Engineers with rusty math who know token-by-token language-model generation.
prerequisites: A probability distribution assigns mass to possible next tokens.
The target and draft models have different roles.
objective: Distinguish DFlash's shared-context parallel per-position predictions from a drafter that conditions on its own earlier choices.
scope: Drafting beats 0-6 are mapped. Verification beats are deliberately not certified by the original all-accepted toy trace or bonus-token prose.
assumptions: The three marginals are invented, not measured.
Independent output choices mean factorization with shared conditioning fixed, not absence of shared target context.
The most likely toy path is the, model, works. Sampling and argmax are distinct operations; this example chooses the modal path.
No correctness claim for arbitrary stochastic speculative decoding follows merely from having a bonus token.
unknowns: Original BEATS[7:9] mix agreement, rejection and losslessness prose while VERIFICATION_RESULT is all true. Rejection behavior and a precise stochastic correctness argument need separate review; this contract does not bless that gap.
The K/V-injection detail in BEATS[3] needs a precise architecture-level source locator beyond the inspected paper introduction.
No audiovisual review or learner responses are supplied.

claims.statement: DFlash uses target hidden features as context for a lightweight block-diffusion drafter that predicts a future block in parallel.

evidence.locator: Section 1, paragraph beginning 'In this paper, we introduce DFlash'
evidence.support: The paper describes target hidden features conditioning the draft model to predict future blocks in parallel.

claims.statement: With shared conditioning fixed, per-position draft marginals induce a factorized sequence distribution, not path-conditioned target probabilities.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2, equations (5)-(7) and discussion of per-position marginals
evidence.support: The draft surrogate Q is formed solely from marginals; full path-conditioned probabilities are unavailable from one block-diffusion forward pass.

claims.statement: The modal toy sequence is the, model, works with draft mass 0.1716; it is not guaranteed to match the target.

evidence.support: The largest marginal entries are 0.55, 0.60, 0.52. Their product is independently checked, and the narration warns of target disagreement.

claims.statement: Projected target features are injected as keys and values into every draft layer.
claims.explanation: This is stated in BEATS[3], but the inspected paper introduction supports only target-feature conditioning. Do not mistake that broad support for validation of every-layer K/V architecture.

evidence.support: Records the scene's architecture claim, not independent proof of it.

worked_examples.description: Verify the displayed modal path's product without a model or scene import.

mapping_note: Indices 0-6 match the original storyboard and narration blocks. Verification/closing beats 7-9 remain unmapped pending semantic revision. No stable runtime event IDs exist.

narration.text: A large language model generates tokens one at a time. Each new token requires a full forward pass through the target model. These empty slots represent the future tokens we need.

beats.purpose: A standard drafter fills successive slots.
beats.question: What does a normal drafter do?

narration.text: A standard draft model fills these slots one at a time, just like the target. It's faster per step, but still sequential. Each prediction waits for the previous one.

beats.purpose: All masked positions are predicted in one pass.
beats.question: How does DFlash do it differently?

narration.text: DFlash replaces this with parallel prediction. Instead of filling slots one by one, it masks the entire future block and predicts all positions in a single forward pass.

beats.purpose: Connect target hidden features to shared draft context; architecture details remain a review gap.
beats.question: Where does the draft model get its context?

narration.text: The key insight: DFlash borrows hidden features from the last target pass. These rich representations are projected and injected as keys and values into every layer of the small draft model.

beats.question: What comes out of the draft pass?

narration.text: One forward pass through the draft model produces an independent probability distribution for each masked position. Position one predicts 'the' at fifty-five percent, 'a' at thirty-five. Position two favors 'model' at sixty percent.

beats.purpose: Position two does not condition on the chosen position-one token.
beats.question: Why are these marginals, not conditionals?

narration.text: Crucially, these are independent marginals, not conditional distributions. Position two's prediction doesn't know what position one actually chose. This is the price of parallelism: the drafter can't condition on its own earlier choices within the same block.

beats.purpose: One toy path emerges, without guaranteeing target agreement.
beats.question: How do we pick tokens from these distributions?

narration.text: We sample a candidate sequence from these marginals. For this toy example, the most likely path is 'the', 'model', 'works'. But because the draft used marginals, this path might not match what the target model would actually produce.

transfer_questions.question: If the first chosen token changes from the to a while shared conditioning is fixed, does q2(model) change? What is the draft mass of a model works?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: q2(model) remains 0.60. The path mass is 0.35 times 0.60 times 0.52 = 0.1092.
transfer_questions.justification: Under the explicit factorization, selecting a different first-position outcome does not recompute position-two marginals. Direct multiplication of the three original inputs gives 0.1092; this says nothing about target acceptance.

transfer_questions.question: Does emitting at least one target token prove that any stochastic draft-acceptance rule is lossless?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: No. Progress and distributional correctness are different. Acceptance and correction must preserve the target distribution, or target-driven selection must be specified.
transfer_questions.justification: The example checks only a draft product; it supplies no theorem about arbitrary acceptance rules. A rule that always accepts every draft could still emit a bonus while biasing the preceding output, so the bonus alone cannot prove equality of distributions.
